title: From Player to Master: Enhancing Test-Time Learning of LLM Agents via Reinforcement Learning over Memory
one_liner: Train the memory updater, not just the player, so that a frozen agent improves across repeated interactions because its stored notes become better tuned to future decisions.
lead: Long-running agents often keep a memory of past interactions, but most systems update that memory with fixed prompt rules. MemoPilot instead learns how to update memory through reinforcement learning, using turn-level rewards and turn-level advantage estimates so that the memory written after one interaction helps the frozen base model make better choices later.

problem.h2: Why hand-written memory rules fall short
paras: When an agent plays a long sequence of rounds, the useful information is not only the current observation. The agent also needs a compact record of what the opponent or environment has been doing so far. That memory affects future decisions because later turns depend on patterns seen earlier.

Most memory methods use fixed templates for what to store. That is brittle because the best memory update depends on long-horizon payoff, not only on what seems locally relevant at one turn. MemoPilot learns memory updates directly from downstream success.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Treat memory writing as a sequential decision problem and train it with reinforcement learning so that stored notes are optimized for future performance.

panels.title: 1. The base player is frozen
panels.viz_args: The policy that chooses actions does not change during test-time play
panels.caption: The paper improves behavior by changing memory updates instead of retraining the player.

panels.title: 2. A fixed memory rule writes weak notes
panels.caption: Poor memory hurts later decisions because the player reads those notes on future turns.

panels.title: 3. MemoPilot writes the memory
panels.viz_args: A learned copilot updates the memory after each interaction
panels.caption: The updater becomes a policy that is judged by long-run game results.

panels.title: 4. Turn-level rewards guide learning
panels.viz_args: Use multi-turn rewards and turn-level advantage estimates
panels.caption: Finer credit assignment helps because each memory edit can be judged by how it changes later play.

panels.title: 5. The frozen player improves over time
panels.caption: Better notes produce better later actions even though the underlying player stays fixed.

steps.text: Read the current game state, action history, and existing memory so that the updater knows what happened and what is already stored.
The learned updater writes, rewrites, or drops notes because only some information will help on future turns.
The base model receives the updated memory and chooses the next action so that the effect of the new memory can be measured.
Assign turn-wise rewards so that memory edits receive feedback tied to the outcomes they help create.
Use many rollouts and turn-level advantage estimates so that useful memory edits are reinforced across long interaction sequences.

paras: The paper changes test-time learning from a fixed memory-writing rule into a trained memory-writing policy.

hidden.name: Long-run value of one memory edit
paras: After a single turn, you can see the new memory text, but you cannot directly see how helpful that edit will be several turns later. A memory note may matter only after the opponent repeats a pattern or after the environment reaches a related state.

MemoPilot estimates that delayed usefulness with turn-level rewards and turn-level advantages. That matters because the updater should keep facts that improve future action quality, not merely facts that sound relevant right now.

heat.caption: Darker means the updater judges that memory component as more important for future play.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is how much one memory edit helps future turns because later choices depend on the notes written now.
The method learns credit assignment over memory updates so that the updater keeps information with high downstream value.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: optimize what the player will read later
paras: The frozen player can only act on what is in its context. If the memory is noisy, incomplete, or poorly timed, later decisions remain weak even when the player model is strong. Improving memory is valuable because memory changes the information state seen on every future turn.

Turn-level advantage estimation helps because full-trajectory rewards alone can be too coarse. The updater needs finer signals so that it can distinguish a good note from a bad one within a long multi-turn sequence.

stages.s: Updater policy improves because useful edits get reinforced

math.h2: Train the memory update with turn-level advantage
math.words: A compact view is that the updater should increase the probability of edits whose turn-level advantage is positive and decrease the probability of edits whose advantage is negative. That works because the advantage measures whether a memory edit led to better later returns than expected at that turn.
symbols: how much better or worse a turn's outcome was than expected
future reward collected after the memory update at that turn
the baseline estimate for how that turn was expected to go

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose after turn 4 the updater writes 'opponent repeats scissors after losing with paper.'
Future reward after that edit is 6.
Expected future reward at turn 4 was 3.
The update becomes more likely because it improved later play beyond expectation.

math.note: The actual training rule uses GRPO over rollouts, but this equation captures the paper's core point because memory edits are reinforced when they improve future returns.

charts.title: Fixed memory rules
charts.note: Hand-written memory rules lag because they cannot tune stored notes to the actual long-horizon objective.

charts.title: MemoPilot learned updater
charts.note: The learned updater performs better because it writes memory that is shaped by future payoff rather than by fixed heuristics. The values are illustrative summaries of the reported trend.

items.html: If useful consequences appear many turns later, even turn-level scoring may remain noisy because one edit can interact with many later events.

items.b: The updater can overfit a narrow opponent pool.
items.html: If training rollouts cover only limited behavior patterns, the updater may store the wrong cues for new opponents because it learned shortcuts tied to the training data mix.

items.b: Memory length is still a constraint.
items.html: A good update policy can decide what to store, but it cannot escape hard context limits, so useful information may still be dropped when too many facts compete for space.
The paper is useful because it shows that test-time learning can target the memory writer directly instead of trying to retrain the full player.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a repeated-game environment where the base player is fixed and receives a short memory string before each turn. Compare three systems: no memory, fixed memory rules, and a learned memory updater. Use a game with exploitable sequential patterns so that memory quality matters across many turns.

The demo should show that the learned updater reaches higher long-run win rate because it records opponent tendencies that actually change later decisions. Log the memory after every turn alongside the action and reward so that you can inspect whether the updater is writing compact, useful notes.
demo.closing: The demo must prove that training the memory updater improves test-time learning because better stored notes change future decisions without changing the base player.
